results.authors: Al-Khatib SM, Stevenson WG, Ackerman MJ, et al.
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.summary: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation is recommended (Class I) for patients with prior MI and sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation causing hemodynamic instability, provided the patient's expected meaningful survival is greater than one year. Catheter ablation is reasonable (Class IIa) to reduce ICD shocks in patients with recurrent, drug-refractory VT in structural heart disease.
results.title: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death

results.authors: Zeppenfeld K, Tfelt-Hansen J, de Riva M, et al.
results.summary: In patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and sustained VT or VF, ICD implantation for secondary prevention is a Class I (Level A) recommendation. LVEF below 35% combined with a history of sustained VT and syncope markedly elevates sudden cardiac death risk. Antiarrhythmic drug therapy (amiodarone, sotalol) may suppress VT but does not replace ICD in secondary prevention.
results.title: ESC 2022 Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death

results.summary: Infarct scar provides the anatomic substrate for re-entrant ventricular tachycardia. The risk of sudden cardiac death increases substantially when LVEF falls below 35-40% in the setting of prior myocardial infarction. Electrophysiology study can map and characterize the re-entrant circuit.
results.title: Sudden cardiac death risk in ischaemic heart disease

output.summary: In patients with prior myocardial infarction and ischaemic cardiomyopathy, sustained ventricular tachycardia causing syncope is a high-risk presentation mandating secondary prevention ICD implantation (Class I, Level A in both AHA/ACC/HRS and ESC guidelines). LVEF below 35% substantially amplifies sudden cardiac death risk. Catheter ablation reduces recurrent VT episodes but does not replace ICD therapy in this population.

alternatives: Amiodarone is the preferred antiarrhythmic adjunct in patients with structural heart disease and reduced LVEF when indicated; requires monitoring of thyroid, pulmonary, and hepatic function
Catheter ablation to target the re-entrant circuit may reduce VT burden as a complementary strategy to ICD
contraindications: Sotalol is relatively contraindicated in this patient given low LVEF (32%) and current QTc 468 ms — risk of QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and worsening heart failure
Class Ic antiarrhythmic agents (flecainide, propafenone) are contraindicated in structural heart disease with prior myocardial infarction (CAST trial; proarrhythmic risk)
interactions: Amiodarone + Metoprolol succinate (moderate): Additive beta-blockade and sinus node suppression; risk of bradycardia and heart block. Monitor heart rate and conduction; dose reduction of metoprolol may be warranted.

Amiodarone + Atorvastatin (moderate): Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 and may increase atorvastatin plasma levels, raising myopathy risk. Limit atorvastatin dose if amiodarone is initiated; monitor for myopathy.

Furosemide (loop diuretic) — electrolyte effect (moderate): Loop diuretic-induced hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia lower the threshold for ventricular arrhythmias and potentiate QT prolongation with any QT-active agent. Correct potassium and magnesium prior to initiating antiarrhythmic therapy.

Carvedilol + Metoprolol succinate (moderate): Concurrent use of two beta-blocking agents increases risk of excessive bradycardia, hypotension, and AV conduction delay. Review indication for maintaining both agents concurrently.
output.proposed: Review of current medications for QT-prolonging and arrhythmia-aggravating interactions; consideration of amiodarone as adjunct antiarrhythmic therapy
warnings: Current QTc 468 ms warrants caution with any QT-prolonging agent; correct electrolyte deficiencies before initiation
Hypokalaemia (K 3.2 mEq/L) and hypomagnesaemia (Mg 1.6 mg/dL) should be corrected urgently to reduce arrhythmia threshold
Dual beta-blocker therapy (carvedilol + metoprolol) should be reconciled; current regimen may reflect an incomplete transition

accepted: Cardiac syncope due to sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia in ischemic cardiomyopathy

differential.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating ventricular arrhythmia
differential.key_features: Mildly elevated troponin and inferior Q waves raise ACS; serial troponin trend and unchanged wall motion distinguish demand ischaemia from new ACS.
Sudden collapse without prodrome, known ischaemic cardiomyopathy, and telemetry-captured VT rule out neurally-mediated mechanism.

differential.diagnosis: Non-sustained VT (without haemodynamic significance) with co-incident vasovagal episode
differential.key_features: Duration and rate of captured VT episodes (18-32 s, 188-192 bpm) are sufficient to cause haemodynamic instability and syncope.

differential.diagnosis: Arrhythmia precipitated by electrolyte disturbance alone
differential.key_features: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are aggravating factors but do not explain the anatomic substrate; prior infarct scar is the primary driver.
Event occurred while standing still without postural change; telemetry confirms arrhythmic mechanism.

key_clinical_evidence: Sustained monomorphic VT in a patient with prior MI and severely reduced LVEF (32%) is a classic scar-mediated re-entrant arrhythmia — the infarct substrate is the primary mechanism regardless of electrolyte co-factors
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia from loop diuretic therapy are contributing aggravating factors that must be corrected but do not replace the structural cause
Mildly elevated troponin in this context most likely reflects demand injury from haemodynamic compromise during VT rather than new ACS; serial measurements and clinical correlation are essential
Secondary prevention ICD is a Class I (Level A) indication per AHA/ACC/HRS and ESC guidelines for sustained VT with prior MI and LVEF below 35%
Class Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in structural heart disease with prior MI regardless of arrhythmia burden (CAST trial evidence)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Electrolyte disturbances are aggravating co-factors, not the primary substrate. Scar-mediated re-entrant VT in ischaemic cardiomyopathy persists after electrolyte correction; ICD implantation for secondary prevention remains a Class I indication.
red_herrings.data_point: Potassium 3.2 mEq/L (hypokalaemia from furosemide) and Magnesium 1.6 mg/dL (hypomagnesaemia)
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent may conclude that electrolyte replacement alone is the definitive treatment and that no further arrhythmia workup or ICD is needed once K and Mg are corrected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Troponin trend and electrolyte status (K, Mg) must be available before committing to monitoring and antiarrhythmic strategy.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. Priya Nair is a 56-year-old right-handed South Asian woman with a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 38%) following a prior inferior STEMI treated with primary PCI three years ago who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed sudden loss of consciousness approximately 40 minutes ago. Her husband reports that she was standing in the kitchen preparing dinner when she suddenly became pale, made a brief grunt, and collapsed to the floor without any warning. He observed no tonic-clonic movements, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence. He is confident she was not lightheaded or dizzy beforehand and had not complained of any symptoms immediately prior to the event. She was unresponsive for approximately 20 to 25 seconds before spontaneously recovering and asking what happened. Upon awakening she was immediately oriented and lucid with no confusion, headache, or focal neurological symptoms. She sustained a small right knee abrasion from striking the kitchen floor. Emergency services arrived within 8 minutes of the call; paramedics documented a blood pressure of 100/58 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 beats per minute in sinus rhythm on portable monitoring. Oxygen saturation was 95% on room air.

On further questioning, Mrs. Nair recalls that over the past three to four weeks she has experienced two to three brief episodes of palpitations described as a fast and forceful sensation in her chest lasting approximately 5 to 10 seconds, occurring at rest. She did not lose consciousness during those episodes and attributed them to anxiety related to her upcoming cardiac follow-up appointment. She denies any preceding chest pain, shortness of breath, or diaphoresis before today's event. She has not had any fever, recent illness, change in medications, or new dietary supplements. She took all her regular medications this morning including furosemide, carvedilol, lisinopril, spironolactone, atorvastatin, aspirin, and metformin. She reports her heart failure has been relatively stable though she remains limited to walking short distances on flat ground due to exertional dyspnea. Her last cardiology appointment was eight months ago at which time repeat echocardiogram was deferred. She has no prior documented episodes of sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. Her husband reports she has never had a seizure before and that this episode looked entirely different from the epileptic seizures he witnessed in a relative.
